a389df548db6df1c: This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order.
Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.
On the political front, Chinese president Xi Jinping has ruthlessly eliminated all potential opposition and centralised power in his own hands.

His decimation of the state, party, provincial, and military leadership has left a trail of bodies and resentment, even if the impenetrability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) makes this difficult to establish definitively.
With blood and revenge hammering in their heads (to paraphrase Shakespeare), numerous humiliated and disgruntled former officials could make Xi’s succession, whenever it comes, disorderly.

Cycles of apparent calm leading to chaos are not uncommon in Chinese history. They are intrinsic to what Francis Fukuyama has called the country’s “Bad Emperor” problem, with Mao Zedong and Xi representing the bad emperors of the Communist era.

On the economic front, the outlook is mixed, but downside risks are growing. Where some see an all-conquering powerhouse marrying technology to mass manufacturing, others see an economy dragged into a structural slowdown by population ageing, a prolonged property market slump, rising youth unemployment, and growing hostility to private enterprise.

Making matters worse, the long-standing source of Chinese dynamism—exports—is vulnerable to policy responses from the US and Europe, which are under immense pressure to address the latest China shock.

But perhaps even more worrying is China’s fraying fiscal capacity. Warnings about unsustainable public debt are growing louder everywhere, but the situation in China is distinctive, owing to how it manages—or, rather, fails to manage—taxation.

Few states are as successful as China when it comes to surveilling and controlling the population. But taxes represent a reciprocal bargain with citizens, who accept expropriation as legitimate on the understanding that they will get something in return: stability, public goods, improved standards of living, redistribution, and so forth. That is why wars and even empires can be lost when a state loses its capacity to tax its citizens.
The fate of the Ming and Qing dynasties is telling in this respect. Even discounting for the obvious historical differences, these episodes have faint echoes in developments today.

We recently mapped China’s taxes and revenues since 1952. Two features stand out. First, and somewhat surprisingly, the CPC has not presided over a particularly strong fiscal state. Instead, it has raised a substantial share of resources without explicitly taxing its people.

Until the late 1970s, about half the resources raised came from profits of state-owned enterprises; and in the last two decades, about one-sixth (and as much as one-quarter at its peak in 2020) has come from land sales.
In other words, China has never managed to raise sufficient sums of money via personal income taxation, even during a period of extraordinary economic vibrancy.

Over the last decade, its tax revenues from the personal income tax averaged just 1.2% of GDP. Ironically, a communist state ideologically committed to collective ownership of the means of production has had to raise revenue by divesting itself of that most sacred input, land. Evidently, the CPC can make the Chinese cower in silence, but finds it difficult to reach into their pocketbooks.
The second and even more relevant finding is that, regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for about a decade.

For example, taxes (excluding social-insurance contributions) collapsed by nearly six percentage points between 2012 and 2025, from 18.4% of GDP to 12.6%. These are levels associated with a struggling, lower-middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower.
It is difficult to say how much of this decline is attributable to growth falling below what headline figures indicate, and how much to weakening enforcement capacity.

Either way, it seems that the government grew so reliant on nontax revenues that it found itself with no options when they dried up. Whether it can change course and impose taxes on the population very much remains to be seen.
The Chinese state could find itself triply exposed—to a succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally.

In short, China’s entire growth and fiscal model, along with the social contract between the state and its citizens—coveted stability and material prosperity for restricted freedom and muzzled voice—may be in trouble.
Of course, any warning about China’s potential descent into disorder must contend with the CPC’s remarkable record of coercive control.

A slow bleed of anemic growth, rising restiveness, and deteriorating services is perhaps likelier. But even if the Chinese miracle ends with a whimper rather than a bang, the consequences may well be yet another global shock.
Navneeraj Sharma is an energy economist. Arvind Subramanian is a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
The views expressed are those of the writers and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
f9e22952ba979019: IPOH: For many women, wearing a saree is part of what makes Deepavali feel special. The 6m-long garment carries generations of tradition and elegance - but getting every pleat and fold into place can be another matter entirely.

For those who never quite mastered the technique, fashion designer and tailor S C Kavitha has a simpler answer: pre-pleated and readymade sarees that preserve the look while cutting down the time spent getting dressed.
Kavitha said the styles have become increasingly popular over the past five years, particularly among younger women who may admire the saree but find traditional draping intimidating.

“Teenagers, in particular, often find wearing a saree difficult because they need help putting it on and getting the pleats right,” she told Bernama. "It can take up to an hour, so many prefer simpler outfits like anarkalis, kurtis or modern dresses.”

Pre-pleated sarees offer a middle ground. Kavitha first measures the garment to fit the wearer, then arranges and steam-presses the pleats before securing them in place. Once prepared, the saree can be slipped on and wrapped around the body in about five minutes, without another pair of hands needed to straighten or rebuild the pleats.
Readymade sarees take convenience a step further, with hooks or buckles at the waist that allow them to be fastened much like a kain sarung.

“The wearer only needs to fasten the hooks and drape the pallu over her shoulder, all in less than a minute,” Kavitha explained. “This takes the stress out of getting ready, especially when welcoming guests or heading to the temple.”

That ease has helped broaden the saree’s appeal beyond Deepavali morning. “I get many orders from Malays and Chinese who want to wear sarees to their Indian friends’ weddings, multicultural events or school functions.
"It’s nice to see people from different backgrounds celebrating our diverse cultures.”
Kavitha charges RM30 to RM40 to pre-pleat a saree, depending on the fabric, while tailoring a readymade version costs RM85 to RM90.

Even as she makes the garment easier to wear, she has not given up on the traditional skill behind it. Kavitha also conducts saree-draping classes, including one-day intensive sessions and two-day workshops for those who want to learn the technique properly.
She said mastering the folds still takes patience and hands-on practice, which is one reason she wants to ensure the knowledge is not lost.
“I want my students to learn the technique properly and remember what they have been taught so they can one day pass on their skills to others,” she said.

For some wearers, that may mean learning the traditional method. For others, a few hooks and neatly prepared pleats are enough to make the saree feel less daunting, while keeping its style and grace very much intact.
e78ec685be8f9fc0: PETALING JAYA: Penganalisis meragui Bersatu dapat mencapai sasaran tujuh kerusi untuk PRN Melaka, berdasarkan kedudukan parti itu di negeri tersebut.
Azmi Hassan daripada Akademi Nusantara berkata keberadaan selama tempoh tertentu tidak bererti parti itu mampu memenangi kerusi.

"Muhyiddin Yassin (presiden Bersatu) agak yakin dengan tujuh kerusi. Saya rasa hujah itu tidak realistik, kerana Bersatu 'survive' di Negeri Sembilan juga tapi 23 daripada 24 calon mereka hilang deposit (dalam PRN Negeri Sembilan)," katanya kepada FMT.
Beliau berkata, hilang deposit dikatakan petanda tiada sokongan. "Negeri Sembilan dikatakan sesuatu malapetaka bagi Bersatu. Apa bezanya di Melaka?"
"Bersatu tidak pernah kuat di Melaka sekarang dan juga lima tahun lepas ketika PRN yang lepas," katanya.
Azmi mengulas kenyataan Muhyiddin baru-baru ini, yang yakin Bersatu mampu memenangi tujuh kerusi pada PRN Melaka kali ini. DUN Melaka mempunyai 28 kerusi.
PRN lalu menyaksikan Bersatu memenangi dua kerusi iaitu Bemban dan Sungai Udang. Wakil rakyat masing-masing kini bersama Parti Wawasan Negara.
Pensyarah sains politik di Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia, Syaza Shukri, juga meragui peluang Bersatu untuk mememangi sesebuah kerusi.
Katanya, terdapat kemungkinan persaingan sengit di beberapa kerusi. "Bagi saya, kalau mereka tak hilang deposit 100% dah kira kejayaan," katanya.
Dalam pada itu, Syaza berkata menyertai pilihan raya secara solo memberi peluang kepada Bersatu untuk memperkenalkan parti itu kepada pengundi.
"Mungkin ia memberikan peluang yang lebih baik dalam PRU akan datang," katanya.
Syaza juga berkata, jumlah undi yang dimenangi Bersatu kelak akan menunjukkan sama ada sokongan pengundi Melayu tertumpu kepada satu blok politik sahaja.
c0f8ae477e6d83bd: SHANGHAI: DeepSeek, the Chinese AI disruptor, released striking adoption numbers for its AI agent infrastructure as it continues to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI with an entire swath of applications built around open-source AI technologies.

On Sunday, the Hangzhou-headquartered startup disclosed on X that DeepSeek Harness, its open-source agent application, had reached 1.54 million daily active users by Nov 4, less than three months after its Aug 13 debut.
Daily users were at about 271,000 at the end of September, right after it released a desktop version of the app, based on the number of users connecting to its own servers.

DeepSeek, which jolted Silicon Valley with its low-cost reasoning model R1 last year, is staking claim to the next frontier of the industry: infrastructure for AI agents, software that lets AI act autonomously on a user’s behalf.

DeepSeek is planning an official marketplace where developers can publish plugins and users can discover them. It’s also planning a support programme for plugin creators including token grants, technical assistance and promotional opportunities. No further details have been disclosed.

The new moves reflect a broader shift in the AI industry where the battle for users is increasingly being fought over ecosystems and integration rather than model performance. DeepSeek is positioning Harness as an open, developer-driven agent ecosystem to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic not just on model performance and cost, but on the breadth of applications built around its AI technology.

The AI disruptor is betting that third-party applications and specialised tools will build traction around its open-source AI agent infrastructure and become a decisive source of competitive advantage against Silicon Valley’s proprietary technologies, as the artificial intelligence industry moves beyond chatbots toward autonomous agents.
AI agents carry out multi-step tasks on behalf of the user such as writing and modifying code, analysing files, conducting research and using other tools with minimal human supervision.

Harness’ appetite for computational power is notable. The application is consuming approximately 92 trillion tokens daily, which works out to about 60 million tokens daily for each active user - providing among the first available evidence of AI agents steeply escalating the demand for processing power.

The scale shows that the hunger for compute power in AI agents is vastly higher than that of chatbots, as AI agents run for multiple hours as they read or write code, use other tools and go on the web, all with little human intervention.

The startup is building Harness as a “everything is a plugin” architecture. A plugin adds a special feature to a piece of software without changing it, giving it added functionality. DeepSeek counts about 35,000 plugins and 60% of users have built at least one of them, though the startup said that the sophistication of the plugins varies.

1d06f5e468ad7f32: KUALA LUMPUR: It is a bustling Sunday morning a week before Deepavali, at the SJKT Azad school hall in Butterworth, Penang. The air is filled with lively chatter and the tempting aroma of freshly prepared treats.
About 60 volunteers are hard at work, preparing festive goodies to bring a little joy to those who might otherwise miss out on the celebrations.
It is a heartwarming tradition that has continued for many years, and one that 56-year-old K Kunavathi holds particularly close to her heart.
Blind since she was 12 because of a hereditary condition, Kunavathi may not be able to see the flurry of activity around her, but that has never stopped her from joining in.
She has been a familiar presence at the annual event for the past decade, happily lending a hand wherever she can.
“There is quite a lot of work, but it makes me feel fulfilled. I hope that whoever receives these Deepavali treats will be happy and blessed,” she told FMT Lifestyle.

The Festival of Lights is traditionally associated with the triumph of light over darkness. In Kunavathi’s hands, its spirit also shines through kindness, generosity and the simple act of remembering others.
Kunavathi is a member of the Malaysia Hindhudharma Mamandram (MHDM), a non-governmental organisation dedicated to promoting Hindu values, cultural traditions and community welfare.

For the past 20 years, the organisation has carried out an annual Deepavali initiative started by its former chairman, the late Dharma Pooshanam V Nanda Kumar. The programme helps inmates observe Deepavali according to their religious customs despite being away from their families.
This year, members prepared 4,000 packs of traditional festive treats, including murukku, athirasam and mixture, for distribution to inmates at Penang Prison and Jawi Prison.

Recipients also received gingelly oil, santhanam (sandalwood powder), shikakai (a traditional hair cleanser), kumkum (vermilion powder) and vibuthi (sacred ash) for ritual baths and prayers on Deepavali.

Kunavathi, who sells religious items at the Sri Sitti Vinayagar Temple in Kepala Batas, said she had long been eager to make a difference in the lives of others. After learning about MHDM several years ago, she was inspired to volunteer.
Although her blindness can make certain tasks challenging, she credits her fellow volunteers with always being ready to lend a hand when needed.
MHDM Penang chairman Thanabalan Nanda Kumar describes Kunavathi as spiritual, disciplined and deeply committed to serving others.

He said that despite being the organisation’s only blind member, Kunavathi is always willing to pitch in. She regularly takes part in gotong-royong and charity fundraising activities, and conducts free Hindu religious classes for students aged six to 17.
“Her calm nature and positive attitude make her a very respected person here,” he added.

Kunavathi is also a Penang state-level Thirumurai competition winner, recognised for her recitation of Tamil Hindu devotional hymns. And, for her contributions to the community, she is a recipient of the Pingat Jasa Masyarakat.
This Deepavali, Kunavathi is celebrating with loved ones, some of whom will have travelled from Johor to spend the festive occasion with her.
As for her community work, she hopes to keep spreading joy and kindness for many more years. “Doing charity makes me happy and I really enjoy it," she said.
"We should all try not just to celebrate, but also to help others during festive seasons. I hope everyone has a happy Deepavali."
3e92df4a37cf9fcb: KUALA LUMPUR: Suasana pagi Ahad di dewan Sekolah Jenis Kebangsaan Tamil (SJKT) Azad di Butterworth, Pulau Pinang, cukup meriah dengan suara sukarelawan dan aroma kuih-muih tradisional Deepavali yang baru disediakan.
Kira-kira 60 sukarelawan sibuk menyiapkan juadah istimewa bagi membawa sedikit kegembiraan kepada golongan yang mungkin tidak berpeluang meraikan perayaan itu seperti orang lain.
Program yang sudah menjadi tradisi sejak bertahun-tahun itu amat dekat di hati K Kunavathi, 56.
Walaupun kehilangan penglihatan sejak berusia 12 tahun akibat penyakit keturunan, keadaan itu tidak pernah menghalangnya daripada turut serta dalam aktiviti berkenaan.
Sejak 10 tahun lalu, Kunavathi antara sukarelawan yang tidak pernah ketinggalan menyertai program tahunan itu dan sentiasa bersedia membantu mengikut kemampuannya.
"Walaupun banyak kerja yang perlu dilakukan, saya rasa puas hati. Saya berharap sesiapa yang menerima juadah Deepavali ini akan berasa gembira dan mendapat keberkatan," katanya kepada FMT Lifestyle.

Deepavali yang dikenali sebagai Pesta Cahaya, melambangkan kemenangan cahaya mengatasi kegelapan. Bagi Kunavathi, semangat perayaan itu turut diterjemahkan melalui sikap pemurah, keprihatinan dan kesediaan untuk mengingati mereka yang kurang bernasib baik.
Kunavathi adalah ahli Malaysia Hindhudharma Mamandram (MHDM), pertubuhan bukan kerajaan yang memperjuangkan nilai agama Hindu, memelihara tradisi budaya dan menjaga kebajikan masyarakat.
Sejak 20 tahun lalu, pertubuhan itu menganjurkan program tahunan sempena Deepavali yang diasaskan bekas pengerusinya, mendiang Dharma Pooshanam V Nanda Kumar.
Program itu bertujuan membolehkan banduan menyambut Deepavali mengikut adat dan tuntutan agama masing-masing, walaupun terpaksa berjauhan daripada keluarga.
Tahun ini, ahli MHDM menyediakan 4,000 pek juadah tradisional seperti muruku dan athirasam untuk diagihkan kepada banduan di Penjara Pulau Pinang serta Penjara Jawi.

Banduan turut menerima minyak bijan, santhanam (serbuk cendana), shikakai (pencuci rambut tradisional), kumkum (serbuk merah untuk upacara keagamaan) dan vibuthi (abu suci) bagi kegunaan mandi mengikut adat serta upacara sembahyang sempena Deepavali.
Kunavathi yang menjual barangan keagamaan di Kuil Sri Sitti Vinayagar di Kepala Batas, berkata beliau sudah lama menyimpan hasrat untuk membantu membawa perubahan dalam kehidupan orang lain.
Selepas tahu mengenai MHDM beberapa tahun lalu, beliau terdorong untuk menyertai pertubuhan itu sebagai sukarelawan.
Walaupun masalah penglihatan menyukarkannya melakukan sesetengah tugas, Kunavathi bersyukur kerana sukarelawan lain sentiasa bersedia menghulurkan bantuan apabila diperlukan.
Pengerusi MHDM Pulau Pinang Thanabalan Nanda Kumar, menyifatkan Kunavathi kuat pegangan agama, berdisiplin dan sangat komited dalam membantu masyarakat.
Menurutnya, meskipun Kunavathi satu-satunya ahli MHDM yang tidak dapat melihat, beliau sentiasa bersedia menyumbang tenaga dalam pelbagai aktiviti.
Selain kerap menyertai program gotong-royong dan kutipan dana kebajikan, Kunavathi turut mengendalikan kelas agama Hindu secara percuma untuk pelajar berusia enam hingga 17 tahun.
"Sikapnya yang tenang dan sentiasa positif membuatkan beliau amat dihormati di sini," kata Thanabalan.
Kunavathi juga pernah memenangi pertandingan Thirumurai peringkat Pulau Pinang, yang mengiktiraf kebolehannya melafaz puji-pujian keagamaan Hindu dalam bahasa Tamil.
Beliau turut menerima Pingat Jasa Masyarakat atas sumbangannya kepada masyarakat.
Sempena Deepavali kali ini, Kunavathi tidak sabar meluangkan masa bersama insan tersayang, termasuk beberapa ahli keluarga yang akan datang dari Johor untuk meraikan perayaan itu bersamanya.
Dalam masa sama, beliau berharap dapat terus melakukan kerja kebajikan dan menyebarkan kegembiraan kepada orang lain untuk tahun-tahun mendatang.
"Saya gembira apabila dapat melakukan kerja kebajikan dan memang suka membantu orang lain.
"Kita semua bukan sahaja perlu meraikan perayaan, tetapi juga berusaha membantu orang lain sepanjang musim perayaan. Saya harap semua orang dapat menyambut Deepavali dengan gembira," katanya.
75d902a894841b0a: SAO PAULO: Lewis Hamilton made a subdued exit from Interlagos on Sunday after a weekend to forget at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, the third race in a disappointing 'triple-header’ for Ferrari.

The seven-time champion finished ninth after starting 20th on the grid, two places behind teammate Charles Leclerc, after a rain-hit contest where Ferrari were amongst the also-rans as Mercedes clinched the constructors’ title.
Ferrari remained second in the teams’ standings but needing only three more points that their rival Mercedes cruised to the world title with little concern on the day.
The result saw Hamilton slip from third to fourth in the drivers’ title race behind new champion Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes, Max Verstappen of Red Bull and Mercedes’ George Russell. Leclerc is fifth.

Hamilton, ahead of his 400th Formula One race start, had started the weekend declaring that he and Leclerc had squashed the unrest and tension that lay between them in the team after a first lap tangle in Mexico, but his raised optimism did not produce results.
"It was a really tough day and weekend for the whole team," he said.
"They have done a really great job – especially all the mechanics in switching the engines and making sure the car was as good as it could be."
Hamilton had engine problems on Friday and had to introduce two new units on Saturday as another one failed during final practice. It led to him being penalised and starting 20th.
"I had a great start in the race, but unfortunately the rear tyre just ballooned and over-heated and after that on slicks I was feeling pretty good.
"It was very tricky in these conditions, and we ended up making an extra stop so I had a lot of ground to cover."
He said he spun late in the race because he did not realise how wet it had become.

"I didn’t hear that it was raining more in the first sector and I passed the pit lane, got to turn one and it was wet. So that unfortunately, lost us a couple of places, but otherwise the team did a great job."
a65d4087191e5c63: KAHERAH: Empat penumpang maut, manakala 88 lagi cedera pada Ahad selepas beberapa gerabak kereta api penumpang tergelincir dan terbalik di Wilayah Giza, utara Mesir, lapor Anadolu Ajansi memetik Kementerian Kesihatan negara itu.

2ce749d2184444c3: SAO PAULO: Toto Wolff hailed his Mercedes team on Sunday after adding the constructors' championship to Kimi Antonelli's drivers' title.

Needing to outscore Ferrari by at least three points at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, George Russell finished fourth and Antonelli fifth in a rain-swept Sao Paulo Grand Prix where Ferrari's Charles Leclerc finished seventh and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton ninth.
"It was a very strong beginning of the season that got us over the line - these last few races have been challenging!" said Wolff.
"I'm so proud of the organisation. We've taken a few years to be back on the top spot and not many teams have been able to come back from that situation."

The Mercedes team took to the podium for a post-race celebration of their triumphant season and ninth constructors' crown, which drew them level with Williams in third place in the all-time table behind Ferrari on 16 and McLaren on 10.
"They all deserve it – an incredible year by everyone," Antonelli said.
"Not only all the people here at the track, but all the people back at the factory in Brackley and Brixworth. They've done an incredible year."
Russell said: "The main thing for today is that we got the constructors' championship. It's a huge amount of work from all of the team to achieve that."

McLaren's Lando Norris won the race ahead of four-time champion Max Verstappen and his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar to foil Antonelli's hopes of winning again a week after he became the sport's youngest champion.
b5623db3fc4b9902: From Zander Lim

Recent criminal breach of trust (CBT) prosecutions involving corporate directors, senior executives and individuals entrusted with institutional funds have renewed attention to the distinction between corporate mismanagement and criminal liability.
Among these are recent prosecutions involving former executives of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd and companies associated with Lembaga Tabung Haji.
These cases raise an important legal question: Does an unauthorised financial transaction, breach of corporate procedures or failure of governance necessarily constitute CBT?

In 2026, several CBT prosecutions were reported, including those involving a former senior military officer in relation to RM3 million belonging to the Armed Forces welfare fund; two company directors involving RM10.55 million connected with a glove manufacturing venture; former executives of three companies concerning contractor penalty payments; and the former CEO of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd involving approximately RM37.37 million allocated for a solar photovoltaic project.
The accused persons have pleaded not guilty, and the allegations remain subject to judicial determination.

Although these prosecutions involve different transactions and circumstances, they raise important legal questions concerning entrustment, corporate authority and the element of dishonesty required to establish criminal breach of trust.
What is criminal breach of trust?
In simple terms, CBT occurs when a person entrusted with someone else's money or property dishonestly misuses it.
Under Section 405 of the Penal Code, the prosecution must generally prove three matters:
(a) Entrustment: the accused was given responsibility for, or control over, the money or property.
(b) Misuse: the accused used or dealt with it in a manner prohibited by law.
(c) Dishonesty: the accused acted dishonestly, rather than merely making a mistake or exercising poor judgment.
Section 409 provides heavier punishment where CBT is committed by certain persons, including public servants and agents.
Importantly, not every unauthorised payment or breach of company procedures amounts to CBT. Dishonesty must still be established.
When does mismanagement become a criminal offence?
Companies may suffer financial losses arising from poor investment decisions, inadequate due diligence, improper approvals or failures in corporate governance.
However, a bad business decision is not necessarily a criminal offence.

For example, Illustration (d) to Section 405 recognises that a person who acts contrary to instructions but genuinely believes the decision would benefit the owner of the property may not have committed CBT, although civil liability may arise.
Conversely, Section 409A makes clear that recording a transaction in the company's accounts does not automatically protect a person from criminal liability.
In other words, a transaction is not necessarily criminal merely because company procedures were breached, nor is it necessarily lawful simply because it was properly recorded or approved.
What matters is whether the money or property was dishonestly misused in circumstances falling within Section 405.
Corporate seniority
In corporate organisations, financial decisions often involve several levels of management, including directors, finance departments and authorised signatories.

Holding a senior position does not necessarily mean that an individual controlled every company transaction. Similarly, approving a payment does not automatically establish dishonest misappropriation.

In determining whether CBT has been committed, consideration must be given to the accused's control over the funds, the purpose of the transaction, the scope of authority and whether the evidence establishes dishonest intention.

In cases involving abetment under Sections 107 and 109 of the Penal Code, criminal liability cannot be established merely because an individual occupied a supervisory position or participated in an approval process.
The prosecution must establish the relevant acts and legal requirements constituting abetment.
Criminal liability must be based on the individual's actual conduct, not merely the position he or she held.
The recent CBT prosecutions highlight the importance of proper financial controls, clear approval procedures and accountability in corporate management.
Nevertheless, financial irregularities, breaches of internal policies and unsuccessful business decisions do not automatically amount to criminal wrongdoing.
Ultimately, the distinction between corporate mismanagement and CBT is not determined by the amount of money involved, the seniority of the accused or whether company procedures were breached.
It depends on whether the accused dishonestly misused money or property entrusted to him or her in a manner prohibited by law.
This distinction is essential to ensuring that genuine criminal misconduct is addressed without treating every failure of corporate governance as a criminal offence.
Zander Lim is an advocate solicitor and managing partner of Law Chambers of Zander Lim.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

bb81a080181292fa: Di Malaysia hari ini ada suatu dilema yang mempunyai implikasi besar terhadap bagaimana Islam perlu dipelajari dan didakwahkan. Ia merangkumi isu derma untuk membayar saman fitnah seorang ahli politik dari parti yang dilaungkan sebagai pejuang Islam, dan derma untuk melunaskan denda hukuman rasuah seorang pemimpin parti politik yang melaungkan kaum Melayu sebagai perjuangan utama.

Dari pemerhatian saya, kalau kes fitnah dan rasuah itu bersifat circumstantial atau agak pudar dan banyak lubang pembuktian, saya tidak akan menulis artikel ini kerana derma bagi kedua-duanya boleh saja dihalalkan dari kaca mata perjuangan Islam atau nasional, tetapi dari apa yang saya faham tentang bukti dan pembicaraan kes-kes, semuanya sahih dan terbaik maka tidak ada keraguan dalam proses pengadilan. Namun demikian, derma untuk membayar saman fitnah dan derma untuk bantu bayar denda hukuman rasuah telah dilancarkan. Yang peliknya penjawat rasmi agama, pendakwah terkenal agama dan profesor agama sepi terhadap sama ada praktis sedemikian layak dikaitkan dengan nilai Islam. Maka itu, terpaksalah saya menulis sesuatu sebagai semacam peringatan.

Sebagai seorang yang telah membina kesedaran Islam di Amerika Syarikat sewaktu belajar jurusan seni bina di bawah tajaan JPA, saya telah menambah banyak ilmu tentang Islam melalui pembacaan koleksi hadis seperti daripada Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Muwatta, Tirmidhi, An-Nasai dan Ibn Madjah, serta menelaah tafsiran al-Quran oleh Muhammad Assad, Abdullah Yusof Ali, Hamka dan Abul A'la Maududi. Penelitian peribadi ini membawa saya kepada banyak buku tentang kerohanian, politik dan aspek sosial Islam. Dalam banyak bacaan saya, ayat dari surah al-Baqarah ini menjadi pedoman kepada saya tentang 'politik Islam';

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang-orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang-orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi; dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang-orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang-orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertaqwa. (al-Baqarah ayat 177)

Dari ayat ini saya boleh membina masyarakat yang baik, saya boleh membina hubungan kerohanian dengan tuhan dan saya juga boleh merancang sebuah perbandaran serta seni binanya untuk manusia. Ayat ini cukup meyakinkan saya kepada apa sebenarnya politik Islam iaitu memimpin manusia ke arah kemanusiaan sejati.

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya" memberi definisi 'kebaikan' atau righteousness iaitu bukan sekadar ibadah ritual tetapi merangkumi suatu kesejagatan kemanusiaan di mana orang Islam perlu berkawan dengan semua manusia yang mempercayai konsep ketuhanan, penghakiman akhir, kewujudan malaikat dan pendidikan melalui kitab-kitab lama berkait dengan rasul-rasul yang kita semua umat Islam kena hafal nama dan kewujudan mereka. Kita pun tahu bahawa sejarah rasul-rasul berkait rapat dengan sejarah dan kepercayaan agama Yahudi dan Kristian. Saya memahami bahagian pertama ini sebagai suatu ajakan untuk umat Islam bersaudara dengan penganut dua agama tersebut. Namun demikian kita kini berseteru dengan kedua-duanya dari sudut politik kenegaraan.

"...dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi" bagi saya adalah tentang suatu sistem sosial yang bukan sahaja untuk sesebuah negara yang mengamalkan hukum dan nilai Islam tetapi juga tanggungjawab setiap muslim untuk membantu golongan yang berkeperluan seperti anak yatim piatu, musafir, yang meminta dan yang memerlukan bantuan kerana keperitan hidup. Kadang-kadang saya hairan apabila dalam sesebuah bandar yang dipimpin orang Islam ada ribu rakyat homeless berbagai kaum tetapi kita punyai rumah ibadat seperti masjid, gereja, kuil dan sebagainya dalam jumlah beratus buah. Sebagai umat kita lebih suka melihat bangunan ibadat beratus juta kecantikannya tetapi membiarkan yang berkeperluan merana sendiri. Siapa agaknya kena jawab di akhirat nanti.

"...dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertakwa" saya fahami sebagai hubungan peribadi kita dengan Tuhan dalam ibadat khusus seperti bersembahyang, dan merenggangkan kita dengan harta benda sebelum kita menemui-Nya. Umat Islam juga diseru untuk menjadi profesional dalam muamalah perjanjian dan tanggungjawab antara manusia tidak kira dari kaum mana atau agama apa, saya kira.

Dalam surah al-Baqarah ayat 177 jelas tiada berkeperluan kita umat Islam untuk merenggangkan kita dengan harta dan wang demi membantu derma bagi membayar saman fitnah yang jelas terbukti tanpa was-was serta juga menderma kepada pembayaran denda hukuman rasuah yang juga terjelas tanpa was-was proses keadilannya.
Jadi, untuk kita orang Melayu dan Islam kat mana atau 'tang' mana kita nak selit amalan kita untuk menjayakan hidup sebagai Muslim yang sejati dan ikhlas membuat kebaikan?

Kalau parti-parti yang menghadapi musibah lalu ahli dan pemimpinnya menggunakan wang tabung parti sendiri tanpa derma maka boleh juga diterima alasan 'strategi politik' agar tidak hilang kerusi dan tidak merendahkan maruah ahli serta parti, walaupun konsep nilai Islam masih lagi boleh dipersoalkan. Tetapi melancarkan derma dan mengajak 'kebajikan' daripada umat Islam untuk 'membantu' musibah yang al-Quran tidak pernah sebut, itu suatu perkara yang cukup problematic dalam usaha menguar-uarkan Islam sebagai agama kemanusiaan terbaik. Walaupun Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan ada buat fatwa bahawa membantu orang yang didapati bersalah oleh mahkamah hukumnya harus, tetapi ia bersyarat iaitu si pesalah perlu mengaku kesalahan dan bertaubat tidak akan membuatnya lagi. Saya tak dengar pun Dr Siti Mastura Muhammad atau Najib Razak berbuat demikian.
Kalau dulu ada buku 'Dilema Melayu', saya kira tiba masanya ada buku 'Dilema Muslim' untuk sama-sama kita renungkan pengakhiran kita dan negara.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
27266a3605e40fe0: HYDERABAD, Nov 9 — Every 90 seconds, an electric three-wheeler rolls off the production line at an Indian factory, underscoring a transformation that has made the country the largest market for battery-powered auto rickshaws.

At a bustling plant run by Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, workers and robots fit cells into battery packs, attach body panels to metal frames and fix wheels into place, racing to meet demand for vehicles known for navigating the chaotic streets of the world’s most populous country.

In September, more than one in two new three-wheelers sold in India was electric, compared with about 8.5 per cent of cars and 11.6 per cent of two-wheelers, reaffirming its position as the world’s largest electric three-wheeler market.
“Our company has grown six times in its EV penetration in the last five years,” said Mahindra LMM’s chief executive Suman Mishra.
She said adoption accelerated over the past two years as government subsidies, improving vehicle quality and falling operating costs combined to make ownership more attractive.
E-rickshaws first appeared on New Delhi’s streets more than a decade ago, often assembled in roadside workshops using Chinese-made batteries fitted to modified pedal-powered tricycles.
But the sector has since eaten into the market for sturdier fossil-fuel-powered three-wheelers, becoming a major industry as manufacturers such as Mahindra expand their share.
The shift has altered the look and sound of Indian cities.
Across northern India, e-rickshaws now queue outside railway stations and bustling markets, replacing the thumping noise of traditional “tuk-tuks”.
Fuel savings
Mahindra is one of 15 finalists shortlisted for the environmental Earthshot Prize, to be awarded in Mumbai by Prince William on November 17.
For many drivers, however, earnings outweigh environmental benefits.
“Money is coming straight into my pocket,” said Afroz Alam, a 31-year-old driver in Hyderabad who switched from a gas-powered model to an EV this year.
The cost of charging his vehicle saves him several hundred rupees a day, helping repay the loan he took out to buy the more expensive electric version.
“It may seem expensive, but then it levels out with the gas money you no longer have to pay,” he told AFP.
Analysts agree economics is the key driver of adoption, with falling costs of batteries and rising fuel prices widening the advantage of e-vehicles.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Workers assemble electric three-wheelers at a Mahindra Last Mile Mobility factory in India, where a new vehicle rolls off the production line every 90 seconds. — AFP pic
Indian think-tank CEEW estimated in 2025 that petrol three-wheelers cost more than twice as much per kilometre to operate over their lifetime as EVs.
“Rickshaws, which operate continuously throughout the day, accumulate fuel savings rapidly,” said Bidisha Bhattacharya of the Delhi-based Chintan Research Foundation.

The trend has also been welcomed by policymakers in India, which imports most of its oil and natural gas and has scrambled to manage energy costs, since conflict in the Middle East erupted in February.
Climate think-tank Ember said India consumes less transport fuel per capita than China did at a comparable income level in 2012, helped by the spread of cheap solar power and declining battery costs.
“In the race to curb oil imports, India is already far ahead,” Ember said in a recent report.
Yet hurdles remain, with adoption uneven across the country.
‘Battery will fail’
E-rickshaws are common in cities such as Lucknow but far less visible in Mumbai, where limited parking and charging infrastructure complicate ownership.
“In Mumbai, there is no parking at all,” Mishra said.
“So you can park on the side of the road for a (fuel-run) vehicle, but how do you do it for an EV when you have to charge it?”
Supply chains pose another challenge.
Last year, China restricted exports of rare-earth magnets, an essential component in electric motors, forcing several Indian automakers to cut or suspend production.
New Delhi has responded by promoting domestic manufacturing, including battery cells, most of which are still imported from China and South Korea.
“Two players are very close to commercialisation of their cells in India. We have to be patient,” Mishra said.
The bigger question is whether the success of e-rickshaws can be replicated in private cars and, eventually, trucks, which consume far more fuel.
Bhattacharya said commercial fleets could provide the next breakthrough.
When taxis transition to electric power, she said, they would help build the charging networks and consumer confidence.
For drivers already making the switch, the argument remains simple.
“They keep saying the battery will fail,” said Mohammad Ali, 26, who bought an e-rickshaw this year.
“Do a trial, take the vehicle and do it for a day. They don’t know yet how much money we are saving.” — AFP
1d696302cbbd99f3: TOKYO, Nov 9 — When Japan’s “symbol of affordability” Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.

That came after Italian-style family restaurant chain Saizeriya issued an almost grovelling apology as it decided to add ¥20 (RM0.50) to the price of its trademark Milanese Doria, lamenting its “lack of effort”.

The very public angst — including in one of the world’s most recognisable clothing brands — highlights the struggles Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country where decades of deflation have nurtured a consumer class averse to higher prices.
The Bank of Japan last month declared its 2 per cent inflation target had been met, after 13 years of ultra-loose monetary policy.

Measures unveiled in 2013 by then-prime minister Shinzo Abe — and continued by successive governments — were supposed to end a spiral of deflation that had plagued Japan for decades since the mid-1990s.
However, it wasn’t until 2022 — when the Ukraine war triggered a global energy shock — that inflation started flickering back to life in resource-poor Japan.

Then the US-Israel war on Iran saw Tehran choke off the strategic Strait of Hormuz, slashing crude exports from the Middle East and impacting global supply chains, in turn sending company costs soaring.
‘Sorry for our customers’
While firms in most countries have been able to lift prices accordingly — albeit to expected anger — those in Japan have to battle an inherent view that hikes are taboo.
Businesses big and small have found themselves hard-pressed to plough ahead with drastic price hikes to avoid alienating customers.
Decisive increases can be more of a risk for smaller, countryside businesses whose survival often hinges on loyal patronage by regular clients.
Sachi, 68, a ramen shop owner in western Japan’s Okayama region, has been holding off on raising prices despite snowballing costs.

“When I imagine myself suddenly announcing a ¥200 hike, for example, I cannot help but feel guilty and sorry for our customers who have supported us for years,” Sachi, who only gave her first name, told AFP during a recent trip to Tokyo.
“So my thinking is, ‘I would rather persevere myself’. I think lots of tiny businesses are like that, especially in rural areas.”
Uniqlo’s decision to row back on its sock price hike came as it sought to protect its status as a paragon of affordability portrayed in local media.
Saizeriya, whose price increases went far beyond Doria to cover almost all menu items, issued a statement some saw as self-flagellating.
The company’s president even vowed at a news conference to “look for any excuses to lower prices again”, to the amazement of social media users.
Still, the chain kept other items such as wine — a stunningly cheap ¥100 per glass — unchanged because “we want it to be enjoyed casually”, its public relations office told AFP.
‘Insanely high’

Soaring grocery bills have left Japanese households less room to spend on other purchases, from dining out to clothing, even as these businesses grapple with rising labour and material costs of their own.
This is despite recent labour ministry statistics showing real wages in Japan have increased year-on-year for eight consecutive months.
“Food prices are getting insanely high, so I have to increasingly rely on stuff imported from overseas, because homegrown products cost me more,” Tokyo office worker Kazuhiko Sato told AFP.
“I’m also eating out less,” he said.
To make matters worse, the Bank of Japan has embarked on a period of interest rate increases to battle inflation, with borrowing costs at a more than 30-year high and likely to go up again.
Tsutomu Watanabe, the professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of economics, said: “Pay raises are still largely insufficient and not benefiting everyone.”
A similar or even higher rate of inflation permeates other Group of Seven economies, but “wage hikes there have been decent enough to keep spending from weakening”, he told AFP.
Therein lies a key difference from Japan, which essentially remains “a convalescent trying to recover from decades of deflation”, the economist said.
“The pricing power of companies is still pretty much dictated by consumers” in Japan, he said.
He thinks it will be “another three to four years” before Japanese consumers undergo a mentality shift to accept chronic inflation as the natural result of steep wage increases.
“After 30 years of deflation, transitioning to a different regime inevitably takes some time,” he said. — AFP

3ad3cf5236692532: SANTA CLARA: Nvidia said on Sunday it is initiating an independent investigation after a media report alleged CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
In a message to Nvidia employees, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility" for his actions.

The New York Times reported last month that US authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," Nvidia said.
The company said on Sunday that, while its board has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Huang said in a message to employees: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Addressing his colleagues, board, partners and shareholders, Huang said: "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
An Nvidia spokesperson said Huang is "committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption."
Top Republican lawmakers in the US House of Representatives have called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the report.

c6db132144c32013: Diego Radames/GettyThis week, around 80 world leaders – including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – will descend on the coastal Turkish city of Antalya for the annual United Nations climate summit, COP31. For the first time, the summit duties will be shared; Turkey will play host, while Australia leads negotiations. At home, these national leaders have no shortage of issues to contend with: the challenges of AI, major wars and declining trust in democracy. Yet looming over all of them is the existential threat posed by a heating planet. Climate change is a truly global challenge. Greenhouse gases have no respect for national boundaries, and the devastating impacts are being felt everywhere. We don’t have a world government, but we do have processes of international diplomacy to hammer out shared commitments. This is how the world is trying to deal with the climate crisis. It can be easy to be pessimistic, but COP31 can still deliver real progress. In Antalya, countries will consider a global electrification target to hasten the shift from coal, oil and gas toward clean electricity. If agreement can be found, this will be a major step forward. Remind me, what is a COP? When scientific consensus emerged on global warming in the 1980s, countries negotiated and signed a new framework on climate change in Rio De Janeiro in 1992. Since then, diplomats and negotiators have met annually for the UN’s Conference of Parties (COP) to discuss how to address dangerous human-made climate change. These talks have become huge, attended by tens of thousands of delegates every year. This year, the 31st COP is being held in Antalya, Turkey. After three decades of climate talks, countries are turning the tide on emissions. Many are transitioning away from fossil fuels, if not at the speed required. Overall, global emissions held roughly flat in 2025, though lower wildfire and land-use emissions masked continued growth from fossil fuels. Yes, the annual UN climate talks are beset by challenges. The United States has withdrawn completely. Countries are not on track to limit warming to agreed levels. Governments can’t even agree when to release the next report on global warming to guide negotiations. In some ways it’s a miracle these talks achieve anything. Agreements must be reached by consensus and endorsed by 190-plus countries, from petro-states in the Middle East to vulnerable island nations in the Pacific. Consensus is both strength and weakness. When agreements are reached, they have great legitimacy. The 2015 Paris Agreement came after two decades of hard-fought negotiations. The agreement was a monumental achievement. But consensus also means COP decisions tend to be “lowest-common-denominator” outcomes, representing incremental progress. Again and again, politics and diplomacy fall short of what the science says is required. Still, if we take a long view, we can see the UN climate talks have helped avoid the most catastrophic global warming and are transforming economies. A demonstrator holds a banner showing the 1.5°C mark, as demonstrators march past the Reichstag building in Berlin, Germany, in April to protest for renewable energies. The UN has confirmed the world will overshoot 1.5°C in the next few years. Photo by Omer Messinger/Getty Images How the Paris Agreement is working At the heart of the Paris Agreement is the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C above the long-term average. This requires the global economy to get to net-zero emissions by the middle of this century. To get there, countries agreed to set emissions targets and increase these every five years. While these targets are slowly cutting emissions and limiting warming they are still clearly insufficient. Before the Paris Agreement, the world was on track for a cataclysmic 4°C degrees of warming this century. The first wave of emissions targets brought this below 3°C. The 2025 round of targets suggests countries may limit warming to 2.6°C. Every fraction of a degree matters. With more ambitious policies, we could theoretically still peak warming at 1.8C and return below 1.5°C later this century through investment in carbon dioxide removal. However, this would take a radical step-change in ambition. Since Paris, more than 130 countries have set long-term targets to achieve net-zero emissions. Countries have begun to signal the end of the fossil fuel era. At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries agreed to “phase down coal”. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023 they agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”. The task now is to make good on these promises. Taken together, COP commitments act as a market signal. This year, global investment in clean energy hit A$3.2 trillion – twice as much as investment in coal, oil and gas. Renewables also overtook coal as the world’s biggest source of electricity. A new age of electricity For COP31, there is a push for an electrification target of “35 by 35”. Both Turkey and Australia are pressing for a global commitment to increase the share of the energy delivered to consumers by electricity, from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035. It sounds wonkish, but could usher in a new age of electricity. A shift to electric vehicles, electric heating and cooling, and modernised heavy industry will cut emissions while slashing global fossil fuel import bills by $720 billion each year. An electrification target may also be easier to land than agreement to phase out fossil fuels. Ironically, given his support for the oil industry, US president Donald Trump has made perhaps the clearest case for electrification. The US war on Iran has triggered the largest disruption of oil supply in history. Demand for clean energy technologies is surging as countries seek alternatives to volatile fossil fuel imports. The exact form of an electrification target at COP31 will be subject to intense negotiations. Australian climate minister Chris Bowen will have his task cut out for him as chief negotiator. In itself, COP31 can’t deliver a silver bullet for climate action. But if it reinforces international cooperation and moves the dial forward on global electrification, hope remains. Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia

8f08dd85e00a623f: Image generated by ChatGPT
All you need to know is his wife Katie didn’t vote, because she was afraid if she registered her address would be made public and…
As it is, she and Stephen are already living on a military base, to ensure their safety. And if that doesn’t tell you all you need to know…

Isn’t this how it always plays out? The rich/elite separate themselves from the hoi polloi to ensure their theoretical invulnerability. From Versailles to Beverly Park… They fly private, they vacation at resorts you’ve never heard of and…
They’re doing it all on your money. It’s the everyday consumer who keeps the wheels of commerce humming.
So how much power does the public have?

Right now people are fired up. I’ve been living a long time and I’ve never seen anything like this. And all those ancient debates about the red and blue not being able to have a conversation, sit at the same table…those days are through.

Of course there are dyed-in-the-wool bonkers believers on the fringes of both parties. But what we learned on Tuesday is we’re more alike than different. It’s finally safe to invite everybody for Thanksgiving. Because one thing we can all agree on is…
We’re PISSED!

You’re supposed to keep the public quiet, their attention diverted, the last thing you want is focus. But Trump demanded it with his antics. Whether it be shooting people in the street or building his ballroom and even more just getting rich. 90% of voters listed corruption as one of their main complaints, why they voted blue. We haven’t all been on the same page since…
I don’t know when.

And now Trump is sticking it in our eye, by appointing the architect of the policies hated by the public. An outsider from his days in high school. We don’t need the class president, or the captain of the football team, but we do need someone who knows how to get along.
As for Trump himself… He seems to be taking a page from Putin’s playbook. Act like dissent doesn’t matter, and go behind the scenes to enforce your vision.

Now historically in America, at least in modern times, you could get away with your bad behavior, by saying everybody else was doing it. Even worse is drinking from the trough because the rich/elite give you access. What America did on Tuesday, and needs to do more, is say NO!
That’s the essence of morality, the essence of character.
And that’s the only thing that will save us.
Netanyahu would not be saying the election was stolen if Trump didn’t lay the groundwork in 2020. Ditto Bolsonaro.

I’m not saying I’m approving of a mob mentality, but this is something different, the people are mad as hell and they’re not going to take it anymore. Funny how they made that movie back in the seventies and now it’s the public on the bleeding edge as opposed to the film business, which notoriously plays it safe.

But people are hungry for edgy. This is how music lost its power. It became about the brand, grosses and… The most revered acts of all time were not necessarily the ones who hoovered up the most money.
So you’ve got to say no to those checks being offered. For your own benefit. You can’t be above the public, but right down in the pit with people.
This is what the Millers are trying to escape.

But that ship sailed over a decade ago. In today’s world everybody has a voice and everybody is equal. You’re grist for the mill. If you’re too big for your britches, if you’re a lyin’, stinkin’, scumbag, the minions are going to go wild on you online.
Everything we were told was true has been flipped. That the oligarchs dictated and…
Funny how all those companies left California for Texas, what now? Did you see the mayor of Houston just decoupled from ICE? If the police stop undocumented people, they’re not going to alert ICE.
Give the guy credit for adjusting. Unlike Agent Orange.
This is why you play the game, because you never know how it will turn out. No one expected a victory this big, no one expected the country to be this pissed.
So now…
We all want to return to business as usual, stop focusing on Washington, D.C., but before that happens…
We’ve got work to do.
Or as the Stones would say…WE’VE GOT THE TURD ON THE RUN

d470c95746552efd: The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management
Originally published on Global Voices
The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park. Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.

Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.

From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity. From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.

Despite relevant research being conducted in the country, information remains limited. According to Delance, some of the available studies on Dominican deep waters have had a geophysical, geochemical, or geological focus, rather than an ecological one. This is largely because deep-sea research is expensive, complex, and requires specialised technology, such as remotely operated vehicles, acoustic equipment, deep-sea cameras, and highly specific taxonomic capabilities.

Precisely because of these limitations, for a long time the National System of Protected Areas lacked a clear representation of deep ecosystems and their underwater geomorphologies, a gap that began to close with the inclusion of the Beata Underwater Ridge as a conservation object within the Orlando Jorge Mera Marine Sanctuary, representing a relevant step forward for the country.

As part of the scientific basis for this process, Delance explains that the technical report on deep-sea fauna documented research between 900 and 4,200 metres deep, recording 1,855 biological observations and 3,294 organisms. One of the most interesting finds was 148 morphospecies, defined in the book Marine Biodiversity as a “group of specimens that can be distinguished from others on the basis of morphological characteristics,” including poriferans, cnidarians, echinoderms, chordates, arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and other yet undetermined organisms.

The pelagic fauna expedition conducted in 2024 covered 2,771 kilometres (1,722 miles) and identified six species of cetaceans, 15 species of birds, as well as sharks and turtle routes. Environmental DNA resulted in the identification of species — including more than 400 morphospecies — along the entire food chain, demonstrating the health and complexity of this space.

Despite these advances, Delance notes, important gaps persist: “We need more information on taxonomic identification at the species level, genetic connectivity, oceanographic dynamics, seasonal distribution, cumulative impacts, biogeography of deep species, and the response of these ecosystems to underwater disturbances, climate change, and other pressures.”
What is deep-sea mining?

According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), deep-sea mining (DSM) refers to the extraction of mineral resources from deposits located on the deep seabed, typically found between 400 metres (1.300 feet) and 6.5 kilometres (4 miles) beneath the ocean’s surface.

There are three primary types of mineral deposits. Polymetallic nodules (PMN) were discovered on March 7, 1873, during the Challenger expedition; scientists described them as “several peculiar black oval bodies which were composed of almost pure manganese oxide.” The ISA states that they are composed of manganese, iron, silicates, and hydroxides, and can be as small as micro-nodules or as large as 20 centimetres. They are commonly found on the west coast of Mexico in the Pacific Ocean (also known as the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone), as well as the Central Indian Ocean Basin, and the Peru Basin. While polymetallic nodules can be found in lakes, the ones with greater economic value are typically located at depths of 4,000–6,000 metres (2.5 miles–3.7 miles), in areas with an extremely low sedimentation rate.

Polymetallic sulphides (PMS), which contain large amounts of copper, zinc, lead, iron, silver and gold, were first discovered in 1948 as part of the Swedish Albatross oceanographic expedition in the Red Sea. Later, in 1963 and 1966, scientists also found metalliferous muds and brines in the Red Sea Rift System.

Finally, cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFC) are found at depths of less than 400 metres (1.300 feet) to more than 5,000 metres (3 miles), mainly in areas with strong volcanic activity. While similar to polymetallic nodules in their composition, these crusts are attracting interest from mining companies because they can contain relatively high amounts of cobalt, as well as platinum, rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese.
The ISA has signed 15-year contracts with 22 contractors for DSM exploration, with most of them covering PMN, eight going to PMS and five to CFC.

The contractors range from national governments — including South Korea, India, Poland and Russia — to research institutes and private companies. A small number, such as South Korea, India and China’s Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association, hold contracts across more than one deposit type, while the majority have a single contract.
The Dominican Republic’s position

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which opened for signature in Montego Bay, Jamaica, in 1982 and entered into force in 1994, establishes the overarching legal framework governing ocean space, marine scientific research and environmental protection.

A central component of the Convention is the definition of “the Area,” the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. UNCLOS declares the Area and its resources to be the “common heritage of mankind,” and establishes the ISA to administer these resources and regulate their exploration and eventual exploitation.
Between 2020 and 2025, the Dominican Republic had an active participation in the ISA, which is headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica.

At the ISA Assembly (ISBA28) in July 2023, Edward Pérez Reyes, the Dominican Republic’s then representative to the ISA, who twice served as its vice president, presented the country’s position on deep-sea mining. While he recognised the importance of these minerals for an energy transition, the DR advocated for a moratorium until there was a solid legal framework and sufficient scientific evidence to guarantee the protection of marine ecosystems. He also proposed sustainable alternatives, the circular economy, and recycling, as well as an equitable distribution of benefits and strengthening of the management of marine resources.

“The Dominican Republic was never against the International Seabed Authority or the process outlined by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” Pérez Reyes, who is now the DR’s ambassador to Japan, explained. “Quite the opposite. We always understood that the international community’s effort to regulate the exploration and eventual exploitation of the seabed was a legitimate exercise. Before that legal framework existed, the risk was that countries with the technological capacity to do so would act on their own. The Convention came precisely to prevent that, and to establish common rules for everyone. So, the discussion was about something else. The question was whether the international community was already in a position to move from exploration to commercial exploitation. Our impression was that it was not yet.”

The DR’s stance, he said — the result of an inter-institutional process involving the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the National Authority for Maritime Affairs (ANAMAR), and more — was never intended to halt the process. Rather, it was to allow science to keep advancing and for the ISA to finish building the regulatory framework that the Convention itself had mandated it to develop. “Every time we learned of a new research study,” Pérez Reyes recalled, “we ended up thinking that there was still much more to know. And that led us back to the same reflection: we had to continue researching before deciding such great consequence.”

Even today, the principles that guided that position still seem valid to him, though the information on which decisions are made can always change. “If science provides new elements, a responsible state has to analyse them,” Pérez Reyes added.

For Delance, scientific exploration of the deep sea is necessary to better understand these ecosystems before considering any form of utilisation. In his view, the DR still lacks key information, including biodiversity baselines, bathymetric and geomorphological maps, data on vulnerable species, ecological connectivity, oceanographic processes, environmental risks, and the resilience of ecosystems.

He believes that the Dominican stance in favour of a precautionary pause in deep-sea mining responds to the need to first generate sufficient scientific evidence to properly plan, regulate, and protect these spaces, and warned that if deep-sea ecosystems are not protected, the DR and wider Caribbean could lose still-unknown biodiversity, genetic resources of potential scientific value, migratory corridors, and essential habitats for threatened species. The country must therefore move, Delance believes, toward marine spatial planning in order to balance conservation and the sustainable use of these strategic ecosystems.
Environmental groups raise opposition

The Magua Ecological Foundation, which is committed to environmental conservation, biodiversity protection, and the sustainable use of natural resources, categorically disapproves of deep-sea mining in the DR, cautioning that the impacts could be severe and irreversible.

Its president, Manuel Alejandro Rodríguez, said that deep-sea mining represents a significant threat to marine ecosystems, whose biological richness and ecological value are fundamental to the well-being of present and future generations. DSM could lead to habitat destruction, species loss, pollution, and disruption of ecological processes, and potentially cause irreversible environmental damage due to the release of metals and other polluting substances into the marine environment.

“In an island nation like the Dominican Republic,” he stressed, “whose seas support extraordinary biodiversity and are essential for activities such as fishing, tourism, scientific research, and the protection of coastal communities, the risks associated with deep-sea mining far outweigh any potential economic benefits.”

Reaffirming the precautionary principle as a fundamental pillar of environmental management, he added, “As long as scientific uncertainties persist regarding the consequences of this activity and there are no guarantees that it can be carried out without causing irreparable damage, it is essential to prioritise the conservation of our marine ecosystems.”

The Foundation wants the authorities, the private sector, scientific community, and society in general to strengthen the protection of our oceans, promote public policies based on the best available scientific evidence, and commit to sustainable development models.

Sixto Inchaustegui, president of Grupo Jaragua, another NGO working for the sustainable management of biodiversity, said that the DR does not know where deep-sea mining activities could take place along its coasts, especially since its continental shelf is very narrow and the country relies heavily on marine and coastal ecosystem services, including tourism, fisheries, and protection against hurricanes. Such ecosystems are already highly threatened and degraded due to land-use changes, mangrove loss, erosion, overfishing, coral mortality, pollution, and other pressures, all of which are being exacerbated by climate change.
New representative to the ISA

On July 14, Ambassador Nancy Patricia Franjul Pérez presented her credentials as the DR’s new permanent representative to the ISA, and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to help develop a solid, transparent, and science-based regulatory framework for the exploitation of mineral resources in the Area.

Franjul Pérez also emphasised the critical role of the ISA at a time when the international community seeks to balance resource security, marine environmental protection, technological development, and the equitable distribution of benefits. ISA Secretary-General Leticia Carvalho said she looks forward to continuing the dialogue, “including on the draft exploitation regulations and the wider work of the Authority, in a spirit of transparency, environmental responsibility, and respect” for the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The future of Dominican marine protection

In 2024, the DR became the first Caribbean country to surpass one of the targets of the global 30×30 environmental commitment, protecting 30.8 percent of its waters. As Delance explained, however, the challenge now is not solely to declare new protected areas, but to ensure they have effective management.

Currently, more than 90 percent of the protected marine area has management plans, a fundamental tool to guide conservation, regulate permitted uses, monitor ecosystems, and support decision-making. Looking to the future, efforts must focus on moving toward effective protection by strengthening monitoring and technological surveillance, regulating maritime traffic, developing national scientific capacity, and generating more research on deep ecosystems.

The DR will participate alongside Colombia in a scientific mission belonging to the inaugural programme of the REV Ocean, the world’s largest ocean research vessel, which will conduct the Beata Ridge mission in 2027.

The expedition will allow for the study of the deep ecosystems of the Beata Underwater Ridge, generate information on its biodiversity and ecological connectivity, and assess potential threats to strengthen ocean conservation and management. The country will also initiate a marine spatial planning process covering both protected and unprotected areas, enabling better organisation of ocean uses and supporting evidence-based decision-making.

79bae9b71c9a01b9: NEW YORK, Nov 8 — Airlines are installing deluxe seats, enlisting Michelin-star chefs for luxury menu offerings and designing elite airport lounges as the industry bets its future on growing demand for premium travel.

The strategy is expected to accelerate the shrinking share of coach class on many flights, with airlines envisioning as much as 70 per cent of passengers paying for enhanced options, if not first-or business class.
Airlines face significantly higher jet fuel costs due to the Iran war, but view such upselling as a profitable long-term bet.

Business class seats can each take up floor space equivalent to four basic-level seats, but can be priced five or six times higher, said Volodymyr Bilotka, a professor at Purdue University and a specialist in aviation economics.
“Airlines have traditionally been investing quite a lot into the premium offerings because the profit margins are significantly higher,” Bilotka told AFP.

In the most recent quarter, American Airlines said premium revenue increased 18.5 per cent year-over-year, four points better than the main cabin. The boost has been a bright spot in a travel market complicated by the jet fuel spike, American executives said.
“Premium products generate roughly half of the company’s ticket revenue on approximately 30 per cent of seats today,” American said.

Besides the traditional differentiation between the main cabin and business class, customers may now pay as much as $200 for more legroom or the ability to sit at the front of the plane and disembark first.
United Airlines announced in July that it would offer a new Economy Plus option that allows customers to forgo having a passenger in the dreaded middle seat.
United plans to begin this option on some flights at the end of 2026.
In September, JetBlue announced the launch of BlueFirst, a new first-class service on domestic flights.
“Customers are increasingly looking for more premium experiences,” said JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty.
Premium’s steady growth
Since 2020, the number of premium seats on US flights has risen 33 per cent, more than double the growth of mainline seats, according to travel news site Skift.
United Airlines more than doubled its premium-seat capacity between 2015 and 2026, the airline told AFP, adding that it plans additional options, like seats with extra elbow room.
Delta has invested in DeltaOne, a revamped luxury option, with premium wine, “top-of-the line” food like the Wagyu burger and larger screens for entertainment.
To assist with the menu, Delta partnered with Simon Hulstone, chef of a Michelin-star restaurant in Britain, and Andrea Robinson, an award-winning sommelier.
The company plans the service for new Airbus A350 planes, with about 150 premium seats and 161 seats in economy.

“Twenty years ago, 90 per cent of the seats were main cabin,” said Ekrem Dimbiloglu, Delta’s managing director for onboard strategy and experience, adding that the share of premium seats could soon represent as much as 70 per cent on some Delta flights.
No major carrier has so far launched service without any economy seats.
In October, British Airways announced that the top level of the two-tier A380 would be entirely composed of premium seats.

Consultancy Cirium estimates that premium seats among the 42 carriers in the three major airline alliances (SkyTeam, Oneworld and Star Alliance) and Middle East carriers now represent 19 per cent of total volume compared with 17.1 per cent in 2019.

Other new options include giving customers choice among meal options prior to boarding and free Wi-Fi. There have also been a slew of announcements of new and beautified airport lounges, including by Southwest Airlines, which was once known as a discount carrier.

But the increasing tendency of airlines to market to customers who can afford premium amenities could open the door to a discount carrier, although higher fuel costs have added to the challenges facing all airlines. — AFP
414b97ddee29fa7f: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.
