cf403874a276142d: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?
16de4ca3c25d3eed: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects.  In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery.  Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw.  It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time.  When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them.  “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM, a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions.  But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. If that number exceeds a certain threshold, the uncertainty is too high, and UQ-DAAAM will refine the caption by using additional images of the object. It does this using a heuristic, or simple rule, that determines which additional viewpoints will reduce the robot’s uncertainty about the object. For instance, it might choose an image captured a few frames later that clearly shows smoke emanating from the chimney.  The researchers mathematically proved that this heuristic can identify the best frames to select without rerunning the VLM, dramatically reducing the amount of computation.  “The key challenge Nico and Harry had to overcome is how to combine VLMs with uncertainty quantification into something that is running in a fraction of a second on a robot that is moving,” Carlone says. Remembering with confidence Once it has identified additional captions that will reduce its uncertainty about the object, the system uses an LLM to fuse them into a single object description. To boost accuracy, the LLM puts more weight on new captions and those with less ambiguity. This refinement step is able to resolve ambiguities for about 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, while only requiring two additional captions per object. It increased the accuracy of object descriptions by 5 percent compared to the state of the art. UQ-DAAAM also provided more accurate answers to questions about the objects it observed, where it saw them, and when it last encountered them than baseline methods. “Performing this uncertainty quantification procedure across the entire map the robot generates allows it to improve its understanding of what it has observed,” Gorlo says. Next, the researchers want to use UQ-DAAAM to guide different types of robots, like mobile robotic manipulators, and apply their uncertainty quantification techniques to other domains.  In addition, they are studying the use of UQ-DAAAM to identify areas of high uncertainty the robot could revisit to improve its understanding of the environment. They are also exploring uncertainty quantification in systems that predict the future state of a robot’s environment. This research is supported, in part, by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Office of Naval Research. Carlone is currently on sabbatical as an Amazon Scholar; this article describes work performed at MIT and is not associated with Amazon.
2e0612d18143103c: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
1c5f8252381c9e95: Menurut ahli falsafah dan sejarawan Perancis yang terkenal, Pierre Nora; terdapat satu hubungan erat antara sejarah dan memori. Akan tetapi Nora menegaskan, dalam banyak keadaan memori adalah lebih utama dan dalam banyak keadaan mengatasi sejarah. Ini kerana memori adalah pencarian kebenaran yang objektif a search for objective truth atau satu himpunan bagaimana ia pernah terjadi, a recollection of how it really was.

Sedangkan sejarah tidak sebebas memori, dan kadangkala perlu dikendala. Ini kerana sejarah selalunya mempunyai aspek ideologi dan boleh dimanipulasi, ideological and manipulative. Idea dan gagasan Nora mengenai pertentangan memori melawan sejarah ini boleh ditemukan dalam banyak karya-karya beliau, antara lain The Present. Nation. Memory; Between Memory and History. Problems of Memory Places; World Celebration of Memory; History as Protection from Politics; dan dalam kerja beliau yang paling masyhur, Places of Memory.

Mengapakah Nora lebih berpihak kepada memori berbanding sejarah, sedang beliau adalah seorang sejarawan? Menurut Nora, beliau pertamanya ingin meluruskan semula sejarah dengan membersihkannya dari fakta tertentu.

Fakta-fakta sejarah ini pada Nora telah dimanipulasi oleh agenda politik dan hanya memori secara kolektif yang dapat membetulkan keadaan ini. Nora dalam kerja-kerja akademiknya menyorot bagaimana gerakan politik, pengukuhan identiti kebangsaan Perancis, dan agenda kelompok tertentu boleh mencemarkan sejarah. Tugas sejarawan sebenarnya adalah memelihara atau melindungi memori ini.

Atas alasan inilah Nora melancarkan gagasan beliau yang dikenali sebagai Places of Memory. Bagaimanapun cabaran untuk meluruskan sejarah dengan mencari memori yang benar ini bukanlah mudah, memandangkan memori itu sendiri terputus, tambahan pula tradisi sendiri akan hancur atau ditinggalkan, dan inovasi mengambil tempat sehingga memori kolektif itu sendiri ikut terjejas. Nora menyatakan, memori yang benar hanya datang dari ruang-tempat memori berjejak memory places atau mnemonic places, yang hadir membentuk ruang memori.

Nora menafsirkan konsep places of memory (lieu de memoire) ini sebagai satu fenomena yang signifikan, terzahir ketara atau tidak ketara, yang mana kerana kenekadan masyarakat atau pengaruh zaman telah membentuk sebagai satu lambang warisan untuk bangsa;

Memori kolektif terbentuk oleh kerana memori berjejak ini yang termanifestasi secara benda, fungsi dan lambang. Memori berjejak dalam bentuk benda misalnya adalah monumen, tugu, memorial, perkabungan, penyanjungan, wajah pada stem atau duit kertas, acara yang bersempenakan memori ini, nama jalan; dan lain-lain. Memori yang terputus memerlukan memori berjejak ini supaya dapat diingat kembali dan sekaligus dimurnikan semula sejarahnya. Sesuatu hanya ‘menjadi sejarah setelah memori berakhir, selagi memori dipugar secara kolektif maka sesuatu itu belum menjadi sejarah meskipun sudah berlaku pada masa lampau’; dalam erti kata lain ‘sejarah akan terus hidup jika terus dikenang’.

Harus diingat, memori berjejak Nora selalu dikelirukan oleh ramai sebagai satu tempat, ini kerana terjemahan suntuk place of memory itu dikait dengan physical place, padahal ia telah kehilangan tempat dan lebih kepada simbol atau tanda, kesan, atau jejak.

Saya selalu mengangankan, atau mencita-citakan agar nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail terlekat dalam memori Malaysia, di saat beliau masih bernafas dan masih hidup. Beliau memiliki tempat dalam memori negara. Saya khuatir meletakkannya dalam sejarah. Ini kerana seperti mana dilihat oleh Nora, sejarah boleh mengalami pemesongan. Buku sejarah boleh diubah oleh pihak yang menang. Sejarah boleh dipadam. Tetapi memori misalnya tidak boleh dipadam. Yazid bin Muawiyah sebagai contoh cuba memadam sejarah mengenai cucu Rasulullah. Dia gagal. Ini kerana Zaynab al Kubra, puteri Fatimah dan Saidina Ali menghidupkan memori abangnya itu dengan segar dan harum. Ia menjadikan kesyahidan itu sentiasa hidup.

Sejarah telah membuktikan bahawa wanita di alam Melayu bukanlah kelompok yang pasif atau hanya berdiri di belakang kejayaan seseorang pimpinan masyarakat. Antara fakta dari lipatan sejarah alam Melayu, dapat dikenali sosok seorang Permaisuri bernama Pramodawardhana yang bertanggungjawab di belakang Kerajaan Majapahit dan Pembangunan Borobudur yang inklusif. Dari era kesultanan hingga ke zaman perjuangan kemerdekaan dan era pemodenan dan digital masa kini, wanita Melayu telah memainkan peranan yang amat signifikan sebagai pemimpin, diplomat, pendidik, usahawan, pemikir sosiobudaya, dan tiang seri utama dalam keharmonian nusa bangsa.

Di saat berlakunya krisis dalam masyarakat, wanita terbukti menjadi penyelamat. Seperti dilakukan oleh Tengku Ampuan Intan Tengku Alang Hussain yang menjadi Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan antara tahun 1869-1872 iaitu ketika berlakunya pertelingkahan untuk merebut kuasa. Watak sedemikian muncul lagi di zaman kita, dengan nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail.

Selaku timbalan perdana menteri (2018-2020) dan pemimpin di Kementerian Pembangunan Wanita, Keluarga dan Masyarakat (KPWKM), Wan Azizah ketika itu telah melancarkan Pelan Tindakan Kebangsaan Menangani Punca Perkahwinan Bawah Umur (2020-2025). Pelan ini merangkumi strategi menyeluruh berasaskan lima punca utama yang digariskan menerusi kajian mendalam, iaitu kemiskinan sosioekonomi, kekurangan akses kepada pendidikan, kepincangan maklumat kesihatan reproduktif, kelonggaran undang-undang, serta persepsi dan stigma masyarakat. Saya membayangkan bagaimana kiranya memori Wan Azizah ini disuburkan terus. Dan memori itu diberi nyawa apabila lima punca di atas terus dikaji dan diberi solusi oleh sebuah universiti. Kita ahli akademik mengkaji dan memberi solusi, atas nama Wan Azizah. Berbahagi pahala.

Satu lagi tonggak utama dalam perjuangan pemerkasaan wanita yang sentiasa Wan Azizah tekankan ialah pengiktirafan terhadap golongan suri rumah yang memerlukan perlindungan keselamatan sosial yang sewajarnya. Di tangan beliau lahir program i-Suri dan i-Sayang yang hari ini mesti diteruskan sebagai usaha menangani jurang perlindungan sosial. Kerajaan ketika itu melancarkan Skim i-Suri di bawah Caruman Sukarela Insentif Suri bagi memastikan suri rumah berdaftar dalam sistem eKasih mendapat tabungan hari tua di Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja (KWSP) dengan bantuan insentif kerajaan.

Memori atau legasi kerja bekas timbalan perdana menteri ini mesti dibaja. Ia mesti diberi, bak kata Pierre Nora, sebuah tanah pamah, sebuah watan dan tekad yang dapat menampang places of memory (lieu de memoire) tersebut. Kalau ada rezeki harapnya memori Wan Azizah ini akan dapat ditegakkan di kala beliau masih hidup, dan di kala saya masih berkhidmat sebagai ahli akademik.
Ini hanyalah angan-angan saya. Agar nama Wan Azizah itu abadi, dan mengatasi sejarah. Ia boleh dan Insya-Allah menjadi memori, satu kenangan yang wangi dan lama. Biarkan ia abadi.

36d4af5b6e476e47: From Clement Stanley
Malaysian Indian People’s Party, a Perikatan Nasional component, decided to skip the Melaka state election as a matter of principle, or so they say.
MIPP president P Punithan said the party would not compromise its principles simply to secure seats in the Nov 14 polls.

MIPP’s struggle, he declares, is to defend the interests of the Indian community with dignity and principles, and “that the community’s voice and interests deserve proper recognition and representation in the political landscape”.
In short, MIPP likely does not want to be seen as token for the opposition coalition’s supposed inclusiveness.
Which, in essence is fine. After all, how can a party market itself as an outfit that champions the Indian cause when it finds itself marginalised?
It is just horrible branding — apart from the fact they lost their deposits in the Johor election — which could be a factor as to why seat negotiations failed.
Yet, MIPP’s dilemma is also, to a certain extent, MIC’s.
What role does MIC play in the bigger scheme of things with respect to its affiliation with Barisan Nasional?
Would MIC be willing to accept the fact that it is by and large irrelevant and a “diversity hire” of sorts?
Are they content being pliant to Umno, BN’s lynchpin, since such an arrangement may guarantee a government post?
Or will they only display bravado, via empty threats to quit BN, before the party’s AGM?
To MIPP’s credit, they were brave to acknowledge where they stand in PN. It is now time for the MIC to do the same.
Pliancy and bravado, however, also bring us to MCA.
Mocked as being Umno’s lapdog for the longest time, MCA leaders walked out of BN’s candidate announcement over seat allocations, also over principles.

The party, its president Wee Ka Siong said, cannot be pushed around and deserves to be treated with dignity. Wee also later called out BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on his claim that talks held after the walkout were “positive”.
Whether one believes it was just “wayang kulit”, the bravado eventually secured three seats for MCA to contest at the Melaka election.
But can MCA consider this a win?
The optics will definitely boost its morale.
Perhaps this will give MCA something to build on. Perhaps they believe that by riding on the tailcoats of a BN-PN pact they will win over more Chinese support for the party.
But truth be told, their victory would be somewhat hollow if they won based on the support of the non-Chinese voters.
Be that as it may, MCA must surely know they are no force to be reckoned with amongst the Chinese electorate.
But, if survival is the name of the game, then by all means be indebted to the Malay support for putting them back in a position of power in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now very likely, in Melaka.
MCA now need only ask themselves, “How high?” when told to jump by the likes of Umno and PAS.
Clement Stanley is an FMT reader.

a40b144ab5da56eb: From a layperson’s perspective, following the legal back-and-forth in the Malaysian courts can be rather taxing.
It often appears to be a war of words, legal arguments, constitutional interpretations and courtroom strategies, all aimed at persuading the presiding judge or judges.

Beneath the pomp and pageantry inherited from the British legal system, however, lie issues of profound constitutional significance that may or may not affect our lives today, but could have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

When Malaysia was formed in 1963, several safeguards were negotiated to protect the interests and autonomy of North Borneo (now Sabah). Among these was Point 11 of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report, under the heading tariffs and finance.
It provided that “North Borneo should retain control over its own finances, development and tariffs, with the right to formulate its own taxation policies and raise loans on its own credit”.

One can argue that the spirit and substance of this safeguard are found in the constitutional expression of Article 112C of the Federal Constitution, read together with Section 2(1) of Part IV of the Tenth Schedule and Clauses (1), (3) and (4) of Article 112D.

These provisions form the constitutional basis for Sabah's entitlement to a special grant equivalent to two-fifths (40%) of the net revenue derived by the federal government from Sabah, subject to the relevant constitutional provisions.

Former Sabah minister Yap Pak Leong revived the historical significance of this arrangement, maintaining that the 40% revenue-sharing arrangement was a fundamental condition underpinning Sabah's decision to join in the formation of Malaysia.
"Right from the start, I emphasised this share of 2/5 revenue to be a condition for Sabah to become part of Malaysia.”
He further stressed that without this safeguard being enshrined in the Federal Constitution, Sabah would not have agreed to participate in the formation of Malaysia.

The role Sabah and Sarawak played in forming Malaysia must be recognised, unlike the federated states of Malaya. The Borneo states negotiated separate terms under the IGC, one of which is Sabah’s entitlement to 40% revenue sharing of all taxes collected in Sabah.

From what I understand, the federal government is not objecting to Sabah’s right to the 40% revenue sharing, but to the High Court judgment on Oct 17, 2025, in favour of the Sabah Law Society (SLS), directing the federal and state government to commence a review within a stipulated period.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself promised during the last state election that the government would not appeal the High Court’s decision, but for whatever reasons, it seems he has reneged on that promise to the Sabah people.
On another point, one cannot help but question the position taken by the state government in these proceedings.
Having entered the case as an intervener at a relatively late stage, the state government appears caught between competing legal and political considerations.
Yet, arguably, it should have been at the forefront pursuing Sabah's constitutional entitlement.
The state government possesses the political mandate, institutional authority and constitutional standing to negotiate directly with the federal government.

Rather than allowing the matter to become an extended courtroom battle initiated by SLS on behalf of the people of Sabah, it should be exercising that authority to secure a meaningful and just resolution for Sabah's 47 "lost years".

In another case, another NGO, Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) has taken the federal government to court on February 27, 2025, disputing the validity of the Territorial Sea Act (TSA) 2012, which limits the State's maritime boundary to just three nautical miles.

While the Sabah state government may have its own reasons for not initiating legal challenges regarding Sabah's rights, and Sabahans are not privy to their arguments, it is only fair to ask where the Sabah government stands in relation to these key court challenges.
The position is unlike in Sarawak, where the state government has led similar challenges.

Importantly, after more than six decades since Sabah agreed to become a part of Malaysia, one uncomfortable reality remains: according to official statistics, Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence in the country.
That is a sobering indictment of the development gap that persists despite Sabah's immense natural resources and its contributions to the Malaysian federation.
The legal arguments may continue. Appeals may be filed, constitutional provisions may be debated, and lawyers may argue over jurisdiction, procedures and remedies.
But beyond the courtroom, ordinary Sabahans continue to face the realities of poverty, inadequate infrastructure, water and electricity shortages, and limited economic opportunities.

The fundamental question is this: after more than 60 years in the Malaysian federation, should Sabahans still have to fight in court for constitutional assurances that were meant to protect their interests from the very beginning?

The 40% entitlement should not be treated as a political bargaining chip, nor should its fulfilment be reduced to a battle of legal technicalities. It is a constitutional matter rooted in the historical terms and safeguards surrounding the formation of Malaysia.
It is about justice, constitutional accountability and the future of Sabah.
The people of Sabah have waited long enough. Following Lord Hewart CJ’s well-known dictum, “justice must be seen to be done”.

Memanglah ada sejarah seorang tokoh dan suatu parti itu mengkafirkan Umno tetapi saya, walaupun menjadi ahli parti tersebut, tidak pernah bersikap demikian.

Lebih teruk lagi parti itu mengutip derma jihad untuk mengiyakan fitnah jelas ahlinya ke atas orang bukan Islam yang lain demi ‘perjuangan menegakkan Islam’ dalam negara.

Janganlah kita ghairah sangat bertakbir dan bertempik Islam namun tergadai akhirnya iman dan jiwa kita kepada kemunafikan dan pendajjalan diri kita sendiri di akhir hayat nanti.

c6b1da594a8a831d: Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes. Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments. While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. How Amendment 3 would work Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes. In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters. Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. Who pays the bill? Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments. With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups. Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes. Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees. Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event. In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll. A looming affordable housing crunch? Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing. When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall. From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift. This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis. eeff4737bf340d02: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey WassonAs Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally. Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record. Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%. When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high. Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978. In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs. In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon. Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon. But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon. On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels. Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026. Implications As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war. It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties. Michael A. 31bba1eca5b3b896: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

a7719ef45c037686: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Originally published on Global Voices
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro. Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States. From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.

Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.” After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”

US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “get involved.” The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides. “The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk. In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended. This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations. Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.

Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name. In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry. In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.

During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press. Global Voices gathered the main ones here. Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.
Rachadinha

This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020. Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization. The case was later adjourned. Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

In 2018, after Bolsonaro’s election, a report by the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf) pointed to atypical financial movements in the account of Flávio’s aide, Fabricio Queiroz, an old friend of his father. Queiroz, who was filmed paying for Flávio's daughters’ tuition in cash, was identified as the scheme’s operator. For the Public Prosecution Office, according to UOL news outlet, the scheme was used to cover Flávio’s personal expenses and to increase his patrimony.

There were also suspicions that a chocolate franchise shop, owned by Flávio, was used for money laundering. The investigation found 1,512 cash deposits in repeated amounts between March 2015 and December 2018 at the establishment.

An audio recording found by police in 2024 shows then-president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s attorneys, and Alexandre Ramagem, former director of the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (Abin), currently a fugitive living in the US, allegedly discussing a plan to free Flávio from the investigations through Federal Revenue Service employees.
‘Dark Horse’ and Vorcaro

On May 13, 2026, The Intercept Brasil published a story and an audio recording showing that the movie “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, starring Jim Caviezel, could have been financed by disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. Before the story went out, a reporter from the news outlet asked Flávio about the case. The senator laughed and dismissed the question, saying: “That’s a lie! Where did you get this from?”

Vorcaro is at the center of one of the country's biggest scandals, involving politicians, members of the Supreme Court and other judges, and celebrities, through his bank, Master — its license was approved during Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Vorcaro is investigated for a fraud scheme that caused a BRL 47 billion (around USD 8.7 billion) loss to the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), which backs Brazil's banking system.

The messages published by The Intercept show Flávio negotiating with Vorcaro on WhatsApp. Flávio asked for BRL 134 million (USD 24.9 million) and received at least BRL 61 million (USD 11.17 million). In one of the last messages between them, before Vorcaro was arrested while trying to flee the country, Flávio tells him: “Brother, I am and will always be with you; there is no half-talk between us,” reported TIB.
Since he couldn’t deny their link, Flávio has repeated that the money he negotiated with Vorcaro was “private money for a private movie.”

This is also one of the investigations into Flávio at the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which targets the movie’s financing operation. Despite the movie being filmed in Brazil, Vorcaro sent the money to a fund in the US (Havengate), managed by a friend of Eduardo Bolsonaro’s. The final destination for the money hasn't been confirmed yet.
Willer Thomaz, a friend

Another inquiry investigates Flávio for money laundering and currency evasion, along with his friend Willer Tomaz, a Brazilian lawyer also currently in the US. Tomaz is under investigation for money laundering through betting companies and involvement in another scandal, a fraud scheme at the national pension fund (INSS).
Documents accessed by Brazilian news outlets showed that Tomaz alone moved BRL 5 billion (around USD 930 million) in betting sites and cashed out BRL 200 million (USD 37.2 million).

When Piauí magazine revealed that Flávio had travelled in Vorcaro’s plane with his family, the senator’s first reaction was to say that “fortunately, it was Willer's.” His friend shared the plane’s quotas with a Vorcaro company. Tomaz denied ever meeting with the banker.

In October, O Globo newspaper published that Flávio had been registered as a “master user” on an offshore account under the name of a company managed by Tomaz and registered on Madeira Island, Portugal. This status could give him “significant operational access,” according to the Federal Police. Piauí magazine also says the senator could have been an indirect partner in a betting company based in São Paulo, but controlled by another company registered in Madeira, also linked to Tomaz. Flávio denies it.

Folha de S. Paulo newspaper says that the relationship between Flávio and Tomaz began in 2019. During the COVID-19 parliamentary inquiry commission at the National Congress, two years later, the senator defended Tomaz, calling him a friend. They always denied being business associates, claiming they were only friends.
Ana Clara’s death and the militias

On the morning of February 2, 2021, five-year-old Ana Clara Machado was shot and killed while playing at the doorstep of her home, in Rio de Janeiro. The Military Police denied any confrontation or the presence of narcos in the area where their operation was taking place. Later, the Civil Police identified police officer Bruno Delaroli as the shooter and arrested him. In March, 2026, ICL Notícias, a news website, reported that Flávio Bolsonaro worked on the officer's defense team in the higher courts, trying to avoid a jury trial. Another news outlet, UOL, revealed he worked pro bono. Lula questioned the senator about his motives during a debate on TV Globo.
Also, according to ICL, this wasn’t the only case Flávio advocated for officers accused of killings. Folha says his career as a defense lawyer gained traction after he was elected senator.

During his political life, Flávio has had a long history of links to police officers identified as members of so-called militias — paramilitary groups mostly formed by active and retired officers, carrying out vigilante and organized crime activities in dominated territories. When a state deputy in Rio, Flávio employed at his office the mother and wife of Adriano da Nobrega, an ex-military policeman, linked to a militia known as Crime Office, whose main activities were to execute ordered killings. He also sent parliamentary money to an NGO connected to another police officer involved in the murder of Rio’s city councillor Marielle Franco. According to Piauí magazine, the militia man known as “Peixe” (fish) referred to Flávio as “our senator.”
ICL News says the UN will examine Flávio's links to the militias when analyzing Ana Clara’s case.
Written by Global Voices Brazil
74ed475c846c9cfc: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans. Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second.

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

0a73cffbe155abce: Repeated giving may give the impression that companies care more. useng/iStock via Getty Images PlusPeople tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people. The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team. Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal, a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

416b7eba9f32ddf4: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.
